turns.content: Hmm. I have the family planning call tonight for the lake house. Last summer Karen treated me like free childcare every afternoon, and she's already posted a schedule assuming the same thing this year. I'm leaning toward just pulling out of the rental entirely. It's not worth the stress. Alex wants me to go and set boundaries ahead of time, but I don't know if I have the energy for that fight. What do you think.

I'll check whether we already have context on this lake-house / Karen / Alex situation so the advice actually fits your history. 1/analysis/personal_context.search/query/family lake house rental Karen childcare schedule Alex boundaries pulling out of trip or setting limits before family planning call

I appreciate you looking into the history. I guess I'm just dreading this call tonight. Part of me thinks it's easier to just tell them we're out and let Alex be disappointed than to go through the whole boundary conversation and still end up resentful.

Yeah, that dread makes total sense. You’re not being dramatic. You’re looking at last summer, looking at Karen already posting a schedule like you’re on staff, and your body is going “nope.” That’s information, not weakness.

The trap in the “just pull out vs. have the fight and still be resentful” split is that those aren’t the only two endings. Pulling out *is* a boundary, and it’s allowed. But if you do it mainly to skip the conversation, you can still end up carrying two messes: family fallout *and* Alex feeling like you bailed on the team. The resentment last year didn’t come from speaking up. It came from being used while nobody named it.

The question that actually matters tonight is this: do you believe Karen would honor a clear limit if you and Alex said it once, calmly, and meant it? If the honest answer is no, walking away isn’t avoidance. It’s you refusing a rerun. If the answer is “maybe, if Alex actually backs me in the room,” then the fight isn’t with Karen first. It’s a ten-minute huddle with Alex *before* the call: you’re not the free afternoon, the posted schedule is not the plan, and if that isn’t acceptable, you’re out. Alex wanting you to “set boundaries” only works if Alex is willing to hold them too, not watch you do it alone.

You don’t have to decide “we’re in forever” or “we’re dead to this family” on the call. You can say you’re not committing to the same setup, and you’ll only be in if childcare isn’t assumed. Short, boring, done. If they push, that’s your answer.

If you want, I can help you draft the two versions: the “we’re out” line for Alex, and the “we’ll come only if…” line for the family call.

I hear you. And I think Alex would back me if it came down to it. But that's the thing — I don't trust Karen to honor a limit even if it's stated clearly. Last year I dropped hints, I said I was tired, I made myself scarce, and she just ignored it all. She'd hand me a juice box and disappear.

So if the honest answer is no, she won't respect it. Then walking away is just refusing a rerun, like you said. But Alex will be so disappointed. And there's the deposit.

You’re not stuck between “be the bigger person” and “be the villain.” You’re stuck between a week you already know the ending of, and a hard conversation with the one person who actually matters.

Karen’s not a mystery. Tired, scarce, hints, juice box, gone. That’s not mixed signals. That’s her treating your no as background noise. If you don’t trust her to honor a clear limit, then the family-call “boundary talk” isn’t brave. It’s you agreeing to a rerun with better wording. You already answered that part.

What’s left is Alex and the deposit, and those feel louder because they’re *your* people and *your* money.

The deposit is a sunk cost. It hurts either way. Going doesn’t get it back in any way that counts if you spend the week as unpaid staff and come home fried. You’re not “wasting” it by walking. You’re refusing to pay a second time in labor and resentment.

Alex’s disappointment is real. You don’t have to pretend it isn’t. But you also said they’d back you if it came down to it. So don’t make them find out on a group call. Tell them first, as a team decision, not a veto you sprung: you’re out of this rental because Karen has already assumed the same setup, you don’t believe she’ll stop, and you are not doing last summer again. They can be sad about the lake and still choose you. That’s actually the test of “Alex would back me.” If they only back you *after* you’re already in the house getting handed kids, that’s not backing you. That’s hoping you’ll absorb it.

Disappointing Alex once is a bruise. Going, smiling, and seething is a crack. You already know which one lasts longer.

You don’t owe the family a debate tonight. You owe Alex a clear “we’re not doing this,” then a short line to the group: you’re withdrawing, sorry about the deposit/logistics, you’re not available as childcare. Boring. Final. If they scramble the schedule, that’s their problem to solve without you.

If you want, I can help you say it to Alex in a way that’s firm without sounding like you’re punishing them for wanting the trip.

I appreciate that. But I keep coming back to something my cousin Elena told me. She's a licensed family therapist. She said walking away from people who violate your boundaries is the only truly healthy move — that trying to get them to change just drains you. I keep thinking about that.

Elena’s line is landing because it matches what you already lived, not because you needed a professional to invent the conclusion. Last summer you *did* try the softer version of change-her: tired, scarce, hints. She handed you a juice box and left. That’s not “you didn’t set the boundary clearly enough.” That’s her treating your limit as optional.

So for Karen, Elena is basically right. Trying to get *her* to become someone who honors it is the drain. You don’t owe another semester of that experiment.

What I’d keep separate is this: walking away from *this rental* is not the same as walking away from the whole family as a moral identity. You can refuse the setup without making tonight a referendum on whether Karen is dead to you forever. The healthy move here is declining the job she already posted you for. That’s it.

Alex’s disappointment still sucks, and it still isn’t a reason to re-enroll. Telling Alex “we’re out” isn’t you trying to change Karen. It’s you stopping the rerun and letting the person who *would* back you actually back you, before a group call turns into a negotiation.

Deposit still hurts. It’s already spent either way. Going doesn’t refund it in any currency you care about if you come home used.

You don’t have to win Karen. You don’t have to convert Elena’s advice into a speech. You can just not go.
I think I'm going to tell Alex tonight that I'm out. I'll say we can figure out the deposit separately but I'm not doing another week of being handed juice boxes and abandoned.

That’s a clean call, and it matches what you already know: Karen doesn’t treat a limit as real, and you’re done auditioning for a different ending.

Tell Alex as a decision, not a debate. Something like: you’re out of the rental, the deposit can be a later logistics problem, and you’re not spending another week as the person who gets a juice box and an empty house. You can be sad with them about the lake. You don’t have to reopen whether Karen might be different this time.

If they get disappointed, let that be disappointment. It doesn’t mean you’re wrong. It means they wanted the trip and you’re protecting the week. Those can both be true.

You don’t owe the family a long explanation tonight. Alex first. Short. Done. You’ve already lived the other version.
